extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and researchers in cultural/media studies, humour studies, and related social sciences
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing the ethics and limits of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of humour focused on its ethical and aesthetic dimensions — identifying when humour functions as a public good and when it produces harm, across race, gender, politics, privacy, parody, and performance. Intended for academic critique and teaching in media/cultural studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and Aesthetics of Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is pervasive in contemporary culture and the book 'considers the ethics as well as the aesthetics of humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat humour not only as an aesthetic/artistic phenomenon but as an ethical practice: interrogate intentions, contexts, and effects; ask how style, form and delivery interact with moral and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as public good versus source of harm
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Humour is pervasive in contemporary culture, and is generally celebrated as a public good. Yet there are times when it is felt to produce intolerance, misunderstanding or even hatred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humour, weigh its social benefits (relief, bonding, critique) against potential harms (perpetuating prejudice, inciting hatred, misunderstanding). Consider audience, power relations, and social context in that balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses and limits of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The book 'focuses on the abuses and limits of humour, some of which excite considerable social tension and controversy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where humour exceeds ethical or social boundaries: catalogue types of abuse (e.g., racist or violent jokes), examine sources of controversy, and analyse why certain jokes provoke social tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility and permission to mock
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted review: 'Jokes must be permitted in order to be funny - but are all jokes permissible? What about violently racist jokes, or subtle sexism in television sitcoms? ... They reject the "just a joke" excuse.' Also reflected in chapter title 'Parody and Decorum: Permission to Mock.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a comedic act has (explicit or implicit) permission to target particular subjects; evaluate decorum, audience consent, social norms, and whether 'permission' changes ethical evaluation of mockery or parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic racism and violence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour that invokes race or violence for its representational choices, how it frames targets, whether it normalises or critiques racism/violence, and audience reception. Analyse historical and institutional contexts that shape meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race and ethnicity in popular humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Race and Ethnicity in Popular Humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how jokes draw on, reinforce, or challenge racial and ethnic stereotypes; consider power asymmetries between joke-teller and target; explore intersections with media industries and popular forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and the conduct of politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Humour and the Conduct of Politics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider political functions of humour: satire, dissent, legitimisation, or delegitimisation of actors; assess effects on public opinion, political discourse, and civic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and decorum (permission to mock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Parody and Decorum: Permission to Mock.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse parody's formal properties and the social rules (decorum) that govern when and how parody is acceptable; interrogate legal, cultural, and ethical boundaries of parodic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour competence and social incompetence
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Merry Hell: Humour Competence and Social Incompetence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate competent humour (timing, audience-awareness, craft) from failures that produce social awkwardness or harm. Use examples to show how 'competence' affects ethical evaluation and social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy, embarrassment and social power (in sitcoms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Privacy, Embarrassment and Social Power: British Sitcom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how humour uses embarrassment and privacy invasions; consider how comedic exposure interacts with social power dynamics, consent, and audience positioning—especially in televised formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedies of sexual morality and female singlehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'Comedies of Sexual Morality and Female Singlehood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representations of gender, sexuality, and moral norms in comedy: how humour polices or subverts sexual morality, and how it constructs narratives around single women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguities of comic impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title: 'The Ambiguities of Comic Impersonation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinise impersonation for ambiguity in target, intent, and effect: consider impersonation's potential to ridicule, solidarise, or perpetuate stereotypes, and the boundary between mimicry and offensive caricature.
